---
title: "The starter project, file by file"
---

You have built three apps now, and each one started as a copy of the same
folder. You opened `index.html` and `src/index.ts` and left the rest alone.
From here on you change some of those other files yourself, so this chapter
opens the box.

## The one line that connects two files {#sec-starter-project-experiment}

Make a fresh app from the
[vite-ts-starter](https://github.com/Teaching-HTL-Leonding/vite-ts-starter)
template and name the folder `starter-tour`. Run `npm install` and `npm start`
in it. The browser shows `Hello World!`, with an exclamation mark that
`src/index.ts` glued on.

Open `index.html` and delete this line from the bottom of the `<body>`:

```html
<script src="./src/index.ts" type="module"></script>
```

Save the file. The page reloads and the heading now reads `Hello World`,
without the exclamation mark. Press F12 and look at the browser console. All
that stands there is Vite's own `[vite] connected.` message. Nothing failed,
because nobody asked for your program.

Put the line back and save again. The exclamation mark is back.

That one line is the whole connection between your HTML and your TypeScript.
A page runs the code it names, and nothing else. The browser cannot run
TypeScript at all, so the development server behind `npm start` translates
`src/index.ts` into JavaScript on the way. The `type="module"` part marks the
file as a module, which is what lets it use `import` in a later chapter.

## What is in the box {#sec-starter-project-tour}

Here is the whole starter, seen from above:

```
starter-tour/
├── .agents/skills/     instructions for AI coding agents
├── .vscode/            settings for VS Code
├── assets/             images and SVG files you add later
├── src/
│   ├── index.ts        your program
│   └── vite-env.d.ts   one line of type information for Vite
├── .gitignore          what git leaves out
├── biome.json          formatter and linter rules
├── index.html          the page the browser opens
├── package.json        the project's ID card
├── package-lock.json   written by npm, never by you
├── skills-lock.json    which agent skills the project pulled in
└── tsconfig.json       the promises you make to the compiler
```

## index.html and src/index.ts {#sec-starter-project-html}

`index.html` is the only HTML file in the starter, and the development server
serves it as the start page. Its `<head>` sets the character set and the title
in the browser tab. Its `<body>` holds one heading with the id
`helloWorldHeader`, plus the script line from the experiment above.

`src/index.ts` is your program, all two lines of it:

```ts
const helloWorldHeader = document.getElementById('helloWorldHeader') as HTMLHeadingElement;

helloWorldHeader.innerText += '!';
```

The starter writes `innerText` here. This course writes `textContent`, and on a
heading that holds plain text the two do the same thing. Everything you build
in the next chapters starts in this file.

## package.json, the project's ID card {#sec-starter-project-package}

`package.json` is the file npm reads. Two parts of it matter to you every day.

**`scripts`** gives long commands short names:

```json
"scripts": {
  "start": "vite",
  "build": "tsc && vite build",
  "check": "biome check .",
  "check:fix": "biome check --write ."
}
```

`npm run check` looks up `check` in that list and runs `biome check .` for you.
That is all `npm run` does. `start` is the one name that also works without
`run`, which is why `npm start` starts Vite. `build` runs two programs in a row:
`tsc` checks your types, and only if that succeeds does `vite build` write the
finished page into a folder named `dist`.

**`devDependencies`** lists the tools the project needs while you work on it:

```json
"devDependencies": {
  "@biomejs/biome": "^2.5.10",
  "typescript": "^7.0.2",
  "vite": "^8.2.2"
}
```

Each of those three version strings starts with a `^`. The research box below
asks what that character allows npm to do.

`npm install` reads this list and builds `node_modules` from it. That folder
passes 100 MB in a fresh starter, because every tool brings its own program
files along. Nobody edits it and nobody sends it to anybody. It never goes into
a git repository either, because npm rebuilds it from `package.json` in half a
minute, which is also why the starter you downloaded was so small.

`package-lock.json` sits next to `package.json` and is written by npm. Unlike
`node_modules` it does belong in git, and what npm uses it for is the second
research question.

## tsconfig.json, promises you make to the compiler {#sec-starter-project-tsconfig}

Read `tsconfig.json` as a list of promises. Each option is you telling the
TypeScript compiler "hold me to this", and the compiler complains the moment
you break one. These four are the ones you will meet this year.

* `strict` switches on the whole strict family at once. The one you already
  know from year one is that a variable of type `string` never holds `null`.
* `noUnusedLocals` and `noUnusedParameters` turn a variable or a parameter that
  nobody reads into an error. Half-finished code stops being invisible.
* `noImplicitReturns` says that if one path through a function returns a value,
  every path has to. Forget the `else` branch and you get
  `error TS7030: Not all code paths return a value.`
* `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is the strict option that surprises people, so
  here it is in three lines:

  ```ts
  const names = ['Ada', 'Grace'];
  const first = names[0];
  console.log(first.toUpperCase());
  ```

  That last line does not compile:
  `error TS18048: 'first' is possibly 'undefined'.` An array can be empty, so
  the compiler refuses to believe that position 0 holds anything. Reading
  `names[0]` gives you a string or `undefined`, and the fix is to handle the
  second case:

  ```ts
  if (first !== undefined) {
    console.log(first.toUpperCase());
  }
  ```

One more line explains a habit of this course: `"noEmit": true`. The compiler
only checks your code here and never writes JavaScript, because Vite does the
translating. That makes `npx tsc --noEmit` a full check of every file in `src`,
worth running before you hand work in. The red squiggles in VS Code come from
the same compiler, but only for the files you have open.

## biome.json, one tool for two jobs {#sec-starter-project-biome}

Biome is the formatter and the linter of this course, and you met both jobs
last year. `biome.json` is where this project decides what they do. The
formatter section sets two-space indentation and a line width of 150
characters, and the JavaScript part below it pins the style rules you have been
following by hand: single quotes, semicolons always, trailing commas. The
linter section switches on Biome's recommended rules, which is the set that
caught `var` and `==` for you in year one.

Two commands use that file:

```bash
npm run check
npm run check:fix
```

`npm run check` reports and changes nothing. `npm run check:fix` writes the
fixes it can make safely, which covers everything the formatter owns. A rule
that needs a decision from you is still only reported.

## The .vscode folder {#sec-starter-project-vscode}

`.vscode` holds settings that travel with the project instead of living in your
personal VS Code, and the starter puts two files there.

`extensions.json` lists the extensions this project recommends, Biome among
them. Open the folder in VS Code and it offers to install them; saying yes puts
Biome's squiggles and its formatter into your editor.

`tasks.json` registers `npm run build` as the default build task of the
project, so **Ctrl+Shift+B** runs it without a terminal.

What the starter does not bring is format on save. Turn it on yourself, once
per project, by creating `.vscode/settings.json` with these two lines:

```json
{
  "editor.formatOnSave": true,
  "editor.defaultFormatter": "biomejs.biome"
}
```

From then on every save formats the file you are editing, and
`npm run check:fix` is only for the files you have not opened.

## Four more files {#sec-starter-project-rest}

`.gitignore` lists what git leaves out, and the two entries that matter here
are `node_modules/` and `dist/`. Both are rebuilt from files the repository
already has, so storing them twice would only waste space. Git gets its own
chapter later.

`assets/` is empty on purpose. Pictures and `.svg` files you want to load go in
there, starting in the SVG part.

`src/vite-env.d.ts` holds a single line that teaches TypeScript about the extra
things Vite allows, such as importing a CSS file. Leave it alone.

`.agents/skills/` and `skills-lock.json` are instructions for AI coding agents,
shipped with the project so every agent that opens the folder gets the same
briefing. The chapter on your coding buddy sets one up.

::: {.research title="What package.json says between the lines"}
The exercise below asks you to compare what `package.json` requested with what
npm actually installed, so you need to be able to read both files.

1. `package.json` asks for `"vite": "^8.2.2"`. Which versions may npm install
   for that, and which ones may it not?
2. `package-lock.json` is written by npm and kept in git. What does npm use it
   for, and what goes wrong for a team that deletes it?
3. `package.json` contains a line `"type": "module"`, and the script tag in
   `index.html` carries an attribute `type="module"`. What does the line in
   `package.json` change, and is it the same thing as the attribute?

For the exam, the `^` rule has to be in your head: you will read version
strings without a search engine.
:::

## Exercise: break it on purpose {#sec-starter-project-exercise}

The first four steps below break the project on purpose, and a different tool
answers each break. Work in the `starter-tour` folder from the experiment, with
`npm start` running in the terminal.

1. **Cut the connection.** Delete the `<script>` line from `index.html` again,
   save, and reload the page with the browser console open. Read what the
   console shows and explain to yourself why none of it is an error. Put the
   line back.

2. **Rename the program.** Rename `src/index.ts` to `src/main.ts` and reload
   the page. The terminal where `npm start` runs prints:

   ```
   [vite] (client) Pre-transform error: Failed to load url /src/index.ts (resolved id: /src/index.ts). Does the file exist?
   ```

   The page loses its exclamation mark again. Two fixes work here: rename the
   file back, or point the `src` attribute in `index.html` at `./src/main.ts`.
   Try the second one, watch the page come back, then undo it and rename the
   file to `index.ts` again.

3. **Leave something unused.** Add this line at the end of `src/index.ts` and
   save:

   ```ts
   const clickCount = 0;
   ```

   Run both checkers and compare them:

   ```bash
   npx tsc --noEmit
   npm run check
   ```

   The compiler answers with one line:

   ```
   src/index.ts(5,7): error TS6133: 'clickCount' is declared but its value is never read.
   ```

   Biome answers with a whole block that points at the variable and ends in
   `Found 1 warning.` Find out which `tsconfig.json` option asked for the
   compiler's error, and notice that the two tools disagree about how serious
   an unused variable is. Then delete the line.

4. **Write it badly.** Add these two lines at the end of `src/index.ts`,
   exactly as they stand, with the wrong indentation, the double quotes, and no
   semicolons:

   ```ts
       const greeting =    "hi there"
   console.log(greeting)
   ```

   Run `npm run check`. It prints the file as it thinks the file should look,
   with `-` in front of your lines, `+` in front of its own, and a small dot for
   every space. Now run `npm run check:fix` and open the file. Both lines are
   indented like the rest of the file now. The double quotes have become single
   quotes, and each line ends in a semicolon. Delete the two lines when you are
   done.

5. **Turn on format on save.** Install the recommended Biome extension if you
   have not already, create `.vscode/settings.json` with the two settings from
   this chapter, and restart VS Code. Now put four random spaces in front of a
   line in `src/index.ts` and save. The spaces disappear.

6. **Read what npm did.** Open `package-lock.json` and search for
   `"node_modules/vite"`. The `version` right below it is what actually landed
   in your `node_modules`. Compare it with the `^8.2.2` in `package.json`, then
   add one comment at the top of `src/index.ts` naming both numbers and saying
   why the `^` allowed this one:

   ```ts
   // package.json asks for vite ^8.2.2, npm installed ..., because ^ allows ...
   ```

   Finish with `npm run check` and `npx tsc --noEmit`. Both stay quiet, and
   your page shows `Hello World!` again.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Breaking things is cheap here

Every break here is one save away from being repaired, and none of them can
damage anything outside the folder. Read each message slowly now and it will be
obvious in three months, when it turns up in a project you care about.
:::
